first_impression.reaction: Googled 'travel advisor benefits' because I'm comparing three planners and want to know what I'd actually be paying for. The headline promises things I 'cannot get booking alone', then the intro says 'None of that is out of reach on your own.' That's the honest version, and I'd rather have it, but the headline oversells. I jumped to the FAQ and the 'Questions to ask' list. The list is genuinely useful: fee in writing, insolvency insurance, chargebacks, AUSTRAC registration, all with government sources I can check. The one question I'd ask first, whether the advisor takes a cut from suppliers, isn't on the list. No hype, no 'award-winning', and it admits I may not need an advisor at all. That earns more trust than most planner sites.

journey.quote: None of that is out of reach on your own. It is simply slower, and it lands on you at the busiest point of the year.
journey.reaction: Honest. But it contradicts the title, 'Travel Advisor Benefits You Cannot Get Booking Alone'. Which is it?

journey.section: What does a travel advisor actually do?
journey.quote: What an advisor does not change is your legal footing.
journey.reaction: Good. Most agents imply you're safer with them. This says you aren't, and links the ACCC so I can check.

journey.quote: It turns a spreadsheet of euros, dollars and rupiah into one figure you can actually plan around.
journey.reaction: One AUD figure is convenient, and it's also where an exchange margin can hide. The page warns about margins on transfers but not on the advisor's own AUD quote. What rate is that figure built on?

journey.section: Someone working in your time zone
journey.quote: A week of back and forth can cover one small question.
journey.reaction: Plausible, and I've lived it. No source, but it's not the sort of claim I'd fight.

journey.section: Your consumer rights, booked either way
journey.quote: Booking through an advisor does not give you stronger rights, and it does not take any away.
journey.reaction: That's the line that made me trust the page. They're telling me the catch: agents may only pass on the provider's remedy.

journey.section: What you can book yourself, and where it gets harder
journey.quote: If the trip is just the two of you, a handful of bookings and one currency, you may not need an advisor at all.
journey.reaction: A business page telling me I might not need them. Honest about trade-offs, which is exactly what I look for.

journey.section: Questions to ask before you hire an advisor
journey.quote: How is your fee charged, and will you put it in writing before you start?
journey.reaction: Right first question. But the list never asks the obvious follow-up: do you earn commission or a mark-up from the venues, hotels and suppliers you book? For a generic checklist that's a strange gap.

journey.section: Questions to ask before you hire an advisor
journey.quote: Some banks allow a chargeback if you do not receive what you paid for, and you should not accept contract terms that ask you to give up chargeback rights.
journey.reaction: Practical and protective. A planner site telling me how to protect myself from planners. Good.

journey.section: Questions to ask before you hire an advisor
journey.quote: Do you belong to an industry accreditation scheme, and what does it require?
journey.reaction: The only question with nothing behind it. Which schemes? What should a good answer sound like? Every other item has a reason attached.

journey.section: When the trip is a wedding and a honeymoon
journey.quote: With Wedded Concierge, one Wedded Advisor plans venue, travel, vendors and payments, anywhere in the world, as your single point of contact from start to finish, working in your time zone and quoting in AUD.
journey.reaction: Fine, it's their pitch and it comes after the evidence, not before. 'Anywhere in the world' is a big claim with nothing behind it, so I'd check it.

journey.quote: If it is a simple trip for two, you may manage comfortably yourself. Your consumer guarantees are the same either way.
journey.reaction: Straight answer to 'is it worth it'. No upsell.

journey.quote: The fee is agreed in writing before any work begins, and the advisor confirms inclusions in writing before you commit.
journey.reaction: They've applied their own checklist to themselves. That's the right closing line. Still doesn't tell me how the fee is charged or whether there's a cut from suppliers.

unanswered_questions: When an advisor quotes in AUD, what exchange rate is that figure based on, and can I see the supplier's original currency price alongside it?
Which industry accreditation schemes exist for Australian travel advisors, and what does membership actually require?
How is the Wedded Concierge fee charged: flat, percentage or per booking? (deferred business detail)
Does Wedded Wonderland take a commission or mark-up from the venues and suppliers its Advisor books? (deferred business detail)
Is there a real destination wedding you've planned with the actual budget shown? (deferred business detail)

turn_offs_found.quote: Travel Advisor Benefits You Cannot Get Booking Alone
turn_offs_found.why: The headline oversells, and the body immediately admits none of it is out of reach on your own. The body is right; the headline reads like marketing hiding the catch.

turn_offs_found.quote: With Wedded Concierge, one Wedded Advisor plans venue, travel, vendors and payments, anywhere in the world, as your single point of contact from start to finish, working in your time zone and quoting in AUD.
turn_offs_found.why: 'Anywhere in the world' is a sweeping claim on a page that otherwise sources everything. Mild, but it's the kind of line I'd check against other sites.

would_share_with: My fiancee, the 'Questions to ask before you hire an advisor' section, as the template for our planner comparison spreadsheet
Our Reddit thread, the 'Your consumer rights, booked either way' section, because people keep claiming agents give you extra protection

cta_reaction.quote: If you would like to talk through your wedding and honeymoon, [speak with Wedded Concierge](https://weddedwonderland.com/wonderland-concierge?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=travel-advisor-benefits&utm_content=closing).
cta_reaction.why: The page earned it: sourced, honest that I might not need them, and they hold themselves to the fee-in-writing rule. But my first question to any planner is whether they take a cut from suppliers, and this page doesn't even put that on the checklist. They go in the spreadsheet and I'd send them the eight questions plus a commission one. I wouldn't enquire off this page alone.

top_3_changes: Add a generic commission question to the checklist after 'How is your fee charged, and will you put it in writing before you start?', e.g. ask whether the advisor receives commissions or mark-ups from suppliers and whether they will disclose them. This is advice to the reader, not a claim about Wedded Wonderland.
Bring the title in line with the honest intro: 'Travel Advisor Benefits You Cannot Get Booking Alone' clashes with 'None of that is out of reach on your own.'

In 'Quotes in Australian dollars', add a line telling readers to ask what exchange rate an AUD quote is built on, and give the accreditation question ('Do you belong to an industry accreditation scheme, and what does it require?') a sourced reason like the other seven.

checks.check: Every journey point and turn-off has an exact quote from the draft
Journey types limited to gained_trust, lost_trust, confused, bored, excited, objection
Stayed in character as Daniel (sceptic): FAQ and questions list first, looked for catches, flagged headline overreach and unsupported claims
No invented brand facts; fee basis, commissions and real-budget questions placed in unanswered_questions as deferred, not must-fix
VERIFY markers and HTML comments (fact tags, image slots) ignored
Deferred business details (fee basis, commissions, on-ground team, scale proof, perks, Wedded Privileges) not penalised

open_questions.question: Does the source pack (ACCC or similar) support adding a generic 'ask about supplier commissions' item to the checklist, and is there a source for what the accreditation question should cover?

assumptions: Daniel arrived via Google for 'travel advisor benefits' while comparing three planners, so relevance is 4 and enquiry likelihood is 2.
Deferred business details are not penalised; the suggested commission question is generic reader advice and does not require any Wedded Wonderland fact.
The 3-minute budget covered the intro, FAQ, the questions list, the consumer rights section, the book-yourself section and the closing, with a skim of the six benefits.
